blocks.x: This tape is being recorded at the home of Herb Morand, 1728 St. Philip Street, New Orleans. The date is March 12, 1950.

Herb, when and where were you born? New Orleans in 1905. And you were educated in the public schools in the city? Yes. Well, do you remember when you first got interested in music? Yeah, when I was about 10 years old. Well, how did you get interested? By listening to the bands playing around town? Yeah, different bands go around the halls and listen at them.
When did you first take up an instrument? Well, as soon as I got the price to buy all batted up a cornet.
How old were you then? Well, I guess I was about 10 or 11. And you said you started playing on your own? Yeah. But you did have music lessons later?

Yeah, well, I used to take old-time Victrola and play different records by Lewis and listen at them. And that's the idea of trying to play a trumpet. Well, who was your music teacher when you had one? Well, after I started playing, Professor Chalini. He used to have music classes, 25 cents a lesson. Every Sunday I used to go. I could play, but I couldn't read. So I decided to take up music in order to read.
Well, after you got out of school was when you started to play and earn it for professional purposes. Oh, yeah. Well, did you have your own band or did you play with someone else?

Well, I had my own band. Most of the trumpet players used to form their own band. You know, get a little group up together. Play house parties. Advertisements for dances and different things like that.
Advertisements for dances, was that like riding around in the wagon? Yeah, in a truck. Well, how old were you when you first got your own band?
Well, I guess I was around 16, 15. My brother, he's also a drummer. He learned how to play beat on steps and tin cans. He got large enough to buy them a set of drums.
Well, do you remember anyone else who was in your first band?
Yeah, Lowe Chester's artist, bass player. He's one of the great bass players of New Orleans. He's played with all the different bands. Buddy, Rene, Chris Kelly, and the different bands.
Well, do you remember any of the bands that were playing at the time when you first got interested in music?
Oh, yeah.
What were a few of those?

I remember Buddy P.T., Chris Kelly, Kid Rene, Sam Morgan, and young Sam Morgan's band. Tuxedo, brass, and string band. Do you remember which of those musicians impressed you the most? Well, most of the trumpet players, like Buddy. I used to play second with Chris Kelly.
Who did you think was the best of trumpet players that you've heard in the New Orleans style? Well, I liked Buddy the best.
He featured mostly low notes. No high note, man. What? When it comes from high note, I don't believe nobody could beat Kid Rene. He could go higher than Lewis at one time.
Well, do you remember what places they played at the time? Yeah.

Different halls, like the Franz Ammi, that's at North Robinson and St. Anthony Street. The Economy Hall on the Eastern Line between Villery and Murray. And the Cooperators Hall, known as the Hopes Hall. That's on North Liberty between St. Fort and Dumaine Street. Then there's the Poiseuilins Hall down on Villery near Ennett Street. Then there's the New Hall.
Those were mostly for private dances?

No, public dances. They'd hire the hall and give advertisement for it. They wouldn't give a ball unless they'd have advertisement. No truck. Many as three and four bands would be out on the street on one Sunday. Whenever they'd meet up together, that was a battle of music. What did they do? Try and play each other down for loudness? No, for everything. Sometimes it'd stop the traffic. And the band that would stay there the longest would be considered the winner.
Did you play with any of these big names that you've mentioned?

I used to play with Chris Kelly on many advertising. He's known as the Blues King. And no band couldn't touch him on the street. When he'd get his rubber flush out and start wow-waring the blues, that was all. He'd run Lewis. And then at that time, people was crazy about blues in the Orleans.
Well, did any of those musicians that you spoke of, did any of them help you? Oh yeah, quite a few of them help.
Buddy, he gave me a song at Bafford Boy, that's recorded by the Harlem Hamfets, my Chicago Bunch. He's the one who gave me that song, Bafford Boy.
And I put the words to it and he gave me the music. Now, you said you had your own group when you were about 15 or 16. Yeah. What type of parties and such did you play for?
Well, mostly it would be house parties. People would clear the house of all the furniture and give different birthday parties, weddings, and christenings and different things like that.
Did you play any of the regular public dance halls later on? Oh yeah. Same halls I mentioned before. Those were with the other bands though?
Yeah, different bands.
Well, do you remember the style of any of the musicians that played at the time? Oh yeah. Would you say a little something about that?

Well, I still keep to my same style. Swing and re-bop and everything came out, but I always stuck to good old Yarlene's jazz. Because when you're playing Yarlene's jazz, you don't have to be worried about anything. Just whatever comes in your head you can make.
Well, who were some of the older players around at the time? Were any that had been playing since the real early days still playing?
Yeah, there's quite a few. Mostly bass players, but most of the horn blowers, they passed away.
Do you remember any of the better clarinetists? From when you started out?
Well, as Boyle Banks, we started out together, Albert Boyle Banks. Were there seventh
How about Buddy Petit?
Yeah.
How did Buddy Petit rank as a trumpeter?
Oh, he was great.
He was one of the great trumpeters? Yeah. He never recorded, did he?

No, he never recorded at all. He used to send me on many jobs, because he'd always be late. So he'd send me to play in his place until he came, like, across the lake, over Mandeville, Bita Springs, different places like that, I'd play until he came over on the later train.
You played a lot of out of town jobs?
Yeah, in and out of the state.
Did you go on any tours with stage companies or anything like that?
Oh yeah, that was later on, before I left to go to Chicago.

It was before 1929. Well, do you remember any of the organized bands then, like the old, there's some left even now, like the Tuxedo? Yeah, I remember all those. Well, did their styles differ very much? Well, no. Do you remember anything about Jack Carey?
Oh yeah, I used to play with him a whole lot, Jack Carey, a trombone player.
Was that the, or Jack Carey that the, was the, that the Tiger Rag was?
Yeah, Tiger Rag, he used to say, he used to say, hold that Tiger, and Jack Carey used to drive a wagon and play trombone.
Do you remember much about Oliver? Was he playing in New Orleans at the time?

No, Oliver left when I was a kid, but I do remember when he used to advertise, which we called Ballyhoo, and on a furniture wagon at that time. That was before the trunk. And I used to sit on a tailgate and give out the cyclists for the ball. So I come to know about Oliver.

Well, do you remember many of the trombones from that time? Well, no, I don't, I don't remember many of them. I mean, you spoke of Jack Carey, do you remember Ori? Was he playing down here then? No, he had left too, I think. Or, uh... Did you ever have anything to do with Professor Mineta, Manuel Mineta? Yeah, Old Horse they called him, eh? Yeah.
Well, he inspired me a whole lot. And, uh, used to show me a few things on the trumpet. Yeah.
Was he more of a teacher or a regular musician? He's still teaching today, yeah. Must be pretty old.
And he features blowing the trumpet and the trombone at the same time. I heard him not quite long ago.
Uh, do you remember any of the pianists? Was a jelly roll still in New Orleans at the time?

No, no, he had left a jelly roll. I don't remember much of him. You played, I imagine, a lot of picnics and... Oh, yeah. In the summertime we were playing picnics. At that time the fairground, we used to get picnics at the fairground. That's when I first heard Lewis a whole lot. Uh, you used to have two bands. A brass band and a big hall and a string band and, uh, at least a jazz band and a small hall.
You must, uh, did you play many, uh, any parades and funerals?
Oh, yeah. I used to play different, different bands, marching bands.
In those days, was there enough, uh, were there enough jobs to keep a musician occupied or did the jazz musicians have to have another outside job?

No, at that time, you... There was enough work to keep all the musicians going because there were so many halls running and house parties and parades. Oh, it looked like every couple of weeks in the summer there would be some parade turning out and big picnics and... Big time. Yeah.

You've spoken of the, uh, some of the bigger bands having, uh, a parade band and string band. Now, uh, how do they, how are they different in composition? Well, like, like the tuxedo, they had a brass band and string band, see.
And the Olympia, Imperial.

That, uh, tuxedo, uh, band, was that the Celestan band? Yeah, it was Celestan, yeah. Who were the, did the personnel change any between the string band and the, uh, marching band, or did they just change instruments?

No, they, they add on to the marching band. It's like the, kind of time, the bass, the tuba player would double on string bass. And they'd use the Sam, uh, Celestan always had another trumpet with him. He used two trumpets. Sam trombone.
Did they, uh, ever have any instruments, did they ever have any other string instruments beside the bass, like violin?
No, they had banjo most of the time and guitar.
Uh, did you ever hear, you, uh, knew Bab Frank, the, uh, piccolo player? No, I don't know. Could you, uh, describe anything about a, how, how they band played at a funeral? Do you remember?

Oh yeah, I used to play so many of them. Uh, the, the society that, uh, deceased members belonged to, well they'd meet at one of the halls, like cooperators or the economy, meet the band there and then we'd march around and go to the house where the body was laid out at. We'd stop playing music a couple of blocks from there and we'd wait until, uh, take them out the house and bring them to the church and they'd have the service in the church. We'd have to wait around until sometime, or the last couple of hours waiting for the body to come out. Then we'd march to the cemetery, playing the funeral marches. And after the body is buried, that's where the real fun begins. Well, I- The second line, they'd be waiting.
Just what was the second line? Well, the second line is, uh, a group of people that were in the

of the family and they'd fall and march with the music and dance and they'd do everything. Sometime they'd fight. I have seen eyes three blocks, second line three blocks long. Police, they'd run them. So they'd run them around one corner and soon he'd turn and beat the band at the next corner.
Now what kind of a tune? You played slow going up to the, uh, church?
Yeah, we played mostly church songs going to the church after we leave the cemetery. That's when we'd get off in jazz.
What, uh, could you name some of the tunes that you played? Oh yeah. Especially at funerals, I mean?

Uh huh. A nice St. Louis blues and tiger rag and, at that time, poke chop rag. That's the plenty. Mylonburg joys. At that time, those numbers was famous. And the blues, march time. What were some of the slow tunes you played following the, or rather taking the body to the cemetery? Well, we played a few marches such as, free as a bird, resurrection. stuff

my guard to deed. It required about four or five because it played so slow and marching so slow with it we wouldn't have to play many. After we'd finished the funeral march then we'd double up on it the time you know walk catch up for the

last time. So do they take the body in a hearse or did the pallbearers carry them all the way to the grave? No in a heist, a heist. Well could you give us a little description of what the parades were like?

You mean the street parades? Yes the street parades. Oh well different clubs would turn out and they're all dressed alike, different umbrellas decorated, cigars and plenty to drink. Did you get a second line there too? Oh yeah, anyway there's music even gonna be a second line.
Do you remember just which instruments were in those marching bands like for the funerals and parades?
Oh yeah we'd have highs, three trumpets, a couple of clarinets, E flat clarinets, a couple of trombones, bass horn, snare drum, snare drum, bass drum, alto horn, baritone.
Do you remember any of the whether any of the musicians that played in the marching bands were different from the ones in the dance bands or did they all switch over from one to another?
Some would switch over. It's like the guitar player maybe he'd double on an alto, an alto in the parade, I mean in the brass band. How? And the bass violin player he'd double on bass, horn.
How were wages in those days for things like that?

Oh it was cheap but you couldn't do so much with a dollar. You could go to the market and with a dollar and a half you couldn't carry the stuff away. We used to get highs, the player dads get three dollars, that was top money. Three dollars. Advertisement, there's about two dollars. And then the halls they wouldn't pay more than four or five dollars a band.
Well did the leader get more than the rest of the band?
Yeah the leader always got say a couple of dollars more.
Were there many places with floor shows like they are today? No they didn't have that much.

Just had a straight band? Yeah just straight band. Very few halls had a piano even. Because we used to play up in a sort of a balcony in the halls. About ten feet from the floor. And that would keep the musicians free, people crowding around. And in my young days I knew quite a few musicians and I'd go to the hall and it had a gate, a little door after you go up the stairway. And if they'd let you up there by them, that was a big honor. To go up there and you know sit by them and everybody look up at you. I used to go quite some time, they'd let me blow a song.
Were there, I mean did many of the musicians sit in with each other's bands?
Well they didn't know, they didn't do that much.
No. Were there singers with any of the bands?
No, no singers. Maybe trumpet player, they would sing. Maybe one song a night, it was mostly music.

You played around New Orleans for quite a few years. Do you remember just when you left? Yeah, I left in 29. That is to go to Chicago. I mean was that on your own hook or did you? No, it was on my own. Did you bring a band with you? No, I left by myself. And what did you do in Chicago? Form a band?
Well, I had to play in with different combinations and I had a chance to audition for some recording. What company was that? That was Decker.
Well, you say you got Chicago in 29. Yeah. Now, were there many New Orleans musicians in Chicago at the time? Oh yeah, there was quite a few there. Could you name a few that you knew?

Well, it was like Lewis, he was at Sunset at the time, and Dublin at the Van Dooms here on State Street, and Oliver, he was at the Plantation on 35th Street, and that was my first chance to hear them away from home. And they really treated me well. Lewis even asked me to play a song to do a number at the sunset. That band was too great. I felt kind of shaky sitting up there with great musicians like that.
Did you ever play any of those bands or did you form your own first?

Well, it's like I said, we got together and formed the Harlem Ampets. Well, who was in that group? Well, myself on trumpet, little Horace Malcolm, Horace Malcolm on piano, Odell Rand on clarinet. He played an E-flat clarinet. He was a little short fellow with a little short clarinet. And Joe McCoy on guitar. His brother Charlie McCoy, he played a mandolin. Mandolin on guitar, whatever you call it. I think it's, it's 12 strings on it. He played a band. We had different drummers. P.C. Williams was one. And John Alenji on bass.
Were those all New Orleans men or were there many from Chicago?
No, just John Alenji and myself.
He was the only New Orleans men on the Harlem Ampets. Did they play New Orleans style or?
Well, I tried to get them to play New Orleans style, but it's a kind of hard proposition. Well, how did you? Playing New Orleans style, you'd have to be born here tonight.
Well, Herb, weren't you directly responsible for the formation of the Harlem Ampets? Yeah. And didn't you write a great many of the tunes?
Yeah, a great many of them, yeah.
But you didn't, you didn't get much royalty from Decca from that, did you? No, no.

Decca, like Old Red, was a, was a hit. I went down to Decca Studios to make a, to have an audition. Let them hear the band. Well, at that time, all the boys was anxious to record and everything. So we played Old Red for an audition number and they decided to record it. Well, Joe McCoy and myself, he's the one that sings Old Red, and just called, you know, formed a band together, him and I. And I told them it would be a wrong move to, to do any recording without a contract or anything. So they all decided to go on and record it, so there's nothing I could do. So we recorded Old Red, so they asked us another number to put on the other side. And we made up a blues right in the studio, Lake Providence Blues. While we recorded that in about a month, all over Chicago, Old Red, what you gonna do?
And following, following that you recorded some other tunes that were equally successful. Right.

And this one part I want to say, that song made a lot of money for everybody but the Hollabamparts. If they just had to act fair with us, we would have got a nice piece. So they kept all the royalties. We didn't get nothing.
Just, could you tell us a few details of just when you got the idea to form the Oralman Half Pats and just how you went about organizing the band? Well, after, that was, that was during the,

Oralman Half Pats was formed around 1937, 1936 I think. When I first went to Chicago, it was in 29, and then I was on the side. That's where I recorded the Melrose Brothers. That's when I made Piggler Wiggler and called them title. I think it's on a Paramount record. A vocal, no, a vocalian. And then I left and went up in Michigan playing with Frank Terrace Band and came back to New Orleans. So the Oralman Half Pats was formed after I went back later in 1937. 1936, 37.

Well, Piggly Wiggly, was that your first record with Johnny Dodds? That was my first recording in Chicago. That's... Now, do you remember any of the other tunes that you wrote back around that time? You said you did Old Red. Yeah, we did Old Red and then we did a Dliper song. You wrote that yourself?

No, I just... I didn't write it. Just one of those things, a song you used to sing around Chicago. I really don't know who really wrote it, but I put most of the music to it. I just played my idea of the music, to feel a vibe. I really don't know who the song belongs to, to tell you the truth.
Well, you played... Were the Hamfats the only band you played with when you were in Chicago?

Oh, no, I played with different other, you know, makeup bands. It's like you go on a gig, this musician at high, you know, different... But strange as it may seem, the Harlem Hamfats, we've never played an engagement together outside of recording.
How did the Chicago musicians at that time adapt themselves to playing with the New Orleans musicians in a New Orleans style? Did they take them long to learn or what?

No, it didn't take them long to learn. They liked the New Orleans style very much. But at that time, I don't know what... Call it swing or... I wouldn't know how to describe it as Chicago style. They'd play mostly fast, jumbled up, mixed up music. A lot of special arrangements.
Do you remember the names of any other band you played with in Chicago besides the Hamfats?
Well, just like I say, it's a different get-up band, you know, organized bands.
Jimmy Newton was in Chicago at that time. Did you ever work with Jimmy Newton? No, I never worked with him. He never did use me. I don't know why. How long were you in Chicago?

Right. Well, just like I told you, I went there in 29. I stood there a while and traveled in and out. Then came back. All again, I stayed in Chicago for 13 years. Did you ever get to New York to do any musicians? Yeah. I played in New York before... I went to New York before I went to Chicago. I went to New York in 26. I was playing with Cliff Jackson and his crazy cats at the Capitol Palace on Lenox Avenue. What was the personnel of that band, do you recall? Well, it's kind of hard. I'd have to look it up, you know. Cliff Jackson?
Cliff Jackson.
The piano.

He said, care for his society right now, I think. And were there many New Orleans jazz musicians in New York at that time? No, no, no. What did New York think of jazz on the whole, I mean, at that time? Were there many engagements for jazz bands there?

No, it looked like it was a different style altogether. Couldn't get them to understand Lewis. Just like Lewis, well, whatever he'd play there, he'd go over great. But most of the musicians up there, they was playing that Eastern style, fast music and jumble up.

Most of you were playing, I mean, back then people really danced to the music. Yeah. They didn't just sit around and listen. Yeah, yeah, they danced. Can you name some of the halls and so forth around Chicago at that time that jazz bands were known to play at?

Well, just like I told you, there wasn't many jazz bands. All this jazz in Chicago was played by the musicians from New Orleans. And then they'd be mixed up with Chicago musicians and you can't very well play like you want. With certain numbers they wouldn't know. And most of them read music. They couldn't play without music and all like that.
You said there were a lot of New Orleans musicians in Chicago at that time. Can you, do you know of any reason why so many of them went there?
Well, I guess there was a greater opening for musicians, which is when Yarlene's music slowed up, the different musicians in the Yarlene start traveling around.
That was due to the closing of Storyville, correct?
Yeah.
Then jazz naturally moved straight up the road. Yeah. Well, what were the organized bands at that time around Chicago? Oliver had an organized band of the other ten.
Yeah, Oliver Lewis, Carol Dickerson, Eddie South, he was there. Quite a few.
Do you recall any white musicians around Chicago at that time from New Orleans or that could play in the New Orleans style? Oh, yes.
Tension to. Yeah. At the time, whenever Bob Cross would come through there, and his band like Fazola, Clarinet, and he's from New Orleans.
There's been so many things written about the Oliver Band in Chicago at that time and how great it was. Just how did the Oliver Band impress you?

Well, it was great because it would do you good to go in the plantation in Chicago and listen to a real New Orleans band a thousand miles away from New Orleans. And you'd have to go early unless you wouldn't get a chance to get a seat. There wouldn't be standing room even. Of course, that was on a cabaret style. And right across the street was Lois Hallslaw at the sunset. The plantation was a half a block away.
The Oliver Band was known to have a large repertoire at that time. Do you recall just how Oliver directed the band and how they played and just how their style was?
Well, just like I said, just like a regular New Orleans band, he'd just stomp his foot and hit off. He wouldn't get in front of the record nothing like that. stuff
Do you remember if there was much jazz on the riverboats at those times, or was it earlier?

You mean here or in Chicago? Well, both here and in Chicago. Well, I used to play on a boat in Chicago at the Navy Pier. That's a recreation pier that extends about a mile, I think, out in Lake Michigan. I used to play on a little excursion boat that makes trips from the pier for a half hour. I used to have a four-piece band there. And I had lucky enough to have three New Orleans men in four in the band. We had four pieces. Like Thomas Taylor, he was on drums. And Alcorn, this Alcorn boy, he was on tenor sax. And Sweet William was on the piano. Myself on trumpet.
Did you notice, did many white Chicago musicians take any notice of the New Orleans musicians, all that style at that time, and try to emulate it?

Oh, yeah, they was playing quite a little bit on Clark Street. I used to play on Clark Street, too. I used to play on Clark Street, too. And I used to come around and sit in, and they could play some nice jazz, too. Was Tom Brown in Chicago at that time?
Well, that was before my time. You mean the saxophone? Tom Brown? No, I'm speaking of Tom Brown, the white trombonist from New Orleans.
Oh. Well, I don't remember. I don't remember. Let's see. It's about the end of the road.
Let's see.

Herb, what was the first band with which you left New Orleans? Well, that was Nat Toll's Creole Harmony Kings, a group of New Orleans musicians. We had an engagement to go to Tulsa, Oklahoma, play at the Nails Brothers Pavilion, a colored pavilion there. And after we played there a couple of weeks, the job blew up. We found ourselves stranded in Tulsa. First time I ever left home with a band. What year was that? That was around 1923. And after that job blew up, we were sitting around in Tulsa trying to get a job someplace else. So, a man drove up in a Model T Ford. A couple of the boys and myself were sitting in front of the hotel. Didn't know what to do. We didn't want to come back home with failure. So quick inside of two weeks. So we all decided we'd stick around and try to get a job someplace else. So, as luck had it with us, he stopped in front of the hotel and called me to the car and asked me, Did I know where he could find a certain band he was looking for around Tulsa? So I told him, I said, no, I don't know. I said, but you're talking to an orchestra right here. I said, we just came in from New Orleans and playing at the Nails Brothers swimming pool and the job blew up. He said, well, you're just the fellas we want. I said, I have a good job for you in Devonport, Oklahoma. I guess that's about 70 or 80 miles from Tulsa. So he said, could we hit a band? I said, sure. So we lined up all the boys and went in the lobby of the hotel and gave them an audition. And he was crazy about it. He had a real New Orleans jazz band. Correct. Yeah, so he gave us the tickets and everything. And he had a table set for us and fit for a king. And we ate and everything. So we started to wait that night in the open air pavilion. And we played for the luncheon and supper. And then played that night in the open air pavilion. And we lived in Chandler, Oklahoma. This was about nine miles from Devonport where we was working. And we didn't have no car or anything. When we left here, we were told we went on a train. And he bought us an old-time Dodge touring car for us to make the trip from Chandler to Devonport every night. And we were very된 stuff with stuff like stuff stuff like stuff stuff like stuff We doubled on clarinet once in a while, but we used to battle on the sax. We couldn't get the clarinet player we wanted to leave New Orleans. At that time, the fellows looked like they were afraid to travel from home. It would be a tough job trying to get a musician to leave New Orleans.
That must have been one of the first New Orleans bands in that part of the country.

Yeah, it was. So to popularize Mr. Jack Phillips, that's his name, popularize his restaurant, he had us broadcast over Station, let's see what it is, I have it in the book there. Bristol, Oklahoma. I think later they changed it to the Voice of Oklahoma, which moved to Oklahoma City. Well, that was my first time I ever broadcast.
And that must have been one of the first jazz broadcasts in that part of the country.
Yeah, it was really. He stumbled upon a jazz band just right out of the sky.
What year was that?

1923. And during that time, at the field, the airport field, at least there was, had an airplane there was taking people up for a ride, 350 person. So, I was having a jazz band there. The sponsors of that decided to get the band, told the band to play on the field to attract the customers. And we played there. I still have the circular. I still have the circular.
Well, you had your band there, as I understand. It was something to do with the trumpet, wasn't there? A plane?
Yeah, well, you see, as I said, I still have the circular.
You used to say the band as an advertisement, the means of getting rides on planes.
So, they said, the Creole Harmony Kings will also take a ride. So, he took us up one by one, one of those old model planes.
That was when the airplanes went in the infancy.

So, he told me, the pilot told me to take my trumpet and blow a number. And when he'd get over the little town of Devonport, he would fly low and cut the motor off, so he could hear my horn playing. So, that idea of cutting the motor off, I didn't know he could do that. So, I took my horn and went up, and I played that Washington Lee swing.
Na-na-na-na-na-na-na-na-na-na-na. Na-na-na-na-na-na-na-na-na-na-na-na.

So, I played it and we calmed down all right. So, they took all the rest of the boys up for a ride. So, Tolles, we played a little trick on him. We told the pilot that Tolles said he didn't care what you would do with him when he'd get him up in the plane. There was nothing he could do to scare him. So, the pilot said, that's what he said. He said, well, I'm going to fix him. So, he took the plane up with Tolles in it. The plane looked to be about two foot long, looking at it from the ground. And he did the loop-to-loop. He did tailspin, whatever you call it. He did everything with Tolles. So, when he brought him down, we think that Tolles was going to be mad, and so we could kid him. He told us, he said, you fellas don't know what a real thrill is until you have a plan loop-to-loop with you. You all know nothing about the airplane. And he came down, and it looked like I see him right now smiling and everything.
What about this experience of going to Mexico with the jazz band?

Well, that came up Nat Tolles' father as a bass player and also a cornet player. So, he had been writing Tolles. And when we'd come back to New Orleans, he had an engagement to go to Yucatan, married to Yucatan, Mexico, to play for the carnival season, which would last a week.
What year was that?

That was a sub year, around 1923. So, after we left Devonport, we started booking dances. After our contract was up, we started booking dances, playing theaters all over the state of Oklahoma. We got a booking agent, and we played such theaters like the Rialto in Tulsa. The first real theater I ever played in, and they gave us a nice write-up. It was crazy about the jazz band. And somehow, a lot of disincentions came from the band with the piano player. It caused the band to split up in Bristol, Oklahoma. We split up. Frank Pasley, he went to Chicago.
Bill Matthews.

And we all split up. And Tolles and I, we were just coming back to New Orleans to make that trip with his father to go to Mexico. And we got as far as Shreveport, Louisiana, and by that time, Tolles had been bought a big 57-mile Cadillac. And the car broke down, and he wouldn't leave the car. So, I came home on the train, and I went to see his father. So, his father had difficulty in getting musicians to leave. They was afraid to cross the Gulf on the boat. So, I told him I would leave. So, I had to go to the doctor to be inspected and get passports and everything. So, I left with Nat Tolles' father flying up out in New Orleans. So, we crossed the Gulf and went into Progreso, Mexico. That's the harbor. And the custom officers. We had to catch a train from Progreso to go to Yucatan. At that time, it was a train, an engine that was going wood. And we had a time on that train. So, we played for a Yucatan club there, a real millionaires club.
Well, you and Tolles' father, were they only two on this trip? Or was there a troop? Who was that? You and Tolles' father?
No, no. I was with Nat Tolles' father. He stood in Threeport with his car.
Oh, I see. But you and Tolles' father were the only two on this particular trip. There was a band.
No, Nat Tolles' father's band.
Oh, I see. So, you recall what the personnel of that band was.

Well, I had a little dad on the banjo. A little bit of a short, comical fellow. And we had a regular six-piece jazz band. And at that time, it was the Charleston craze was out. And we had Dancing Pete and his dancing partner. We took them over with us. And the people went wild over the band. Charleston. And we played for the carnival. And we made some nice money on that trip. And it was treated like kings. And I think it's the Spanish Opera. They had their big opera and everything. And we were supposed to come on after the opera. And they had heard our band all around the town. And believe it or not, they started clapping for the Americano jazz. They couldn't wait to listen to the opera. Because they know we was coming on on the end. And after the opera finished, we cared more than we really tore the house down. And our dancing, Charleston, and our jazz music. And we played at the Yucatan Club. And they had a really 75-piece Spanish band. And every time they'd finish playing, we'd play a number and they'd play a number. When they'd finish, they'd all cry around and stare while we was playing that jazz. And some of them had never heard of jazz before, as played in New Orleans. And we were treated just like a king. And everybody came back, had a good time, plenty of souvenirs, money. We all came home with about $500 a piece in gold, which was a lot of money in 1923 for musicians to make. And we stood over our time. We had a certain time to stay there. So they liked us so much. We had so many extra engagements. We used to go play serenading. See, a group of Spanish fellows would hire the band. And we'd go out, say, at 1230 at night to some of their friend's house and strike up the band. And they'd join the party. And we'd go to somebody else's house. And when we'd finish up, we had about 7,500 people dancing on the sidewalk.
Did any of the Spanish musicians ever play with you?
Oh no, no, but I heard a lot of them. They couldn't understand or play jazz, but they're some really good musicians and the sweetest music ever on here.
Well, you were attending New Orleans about 1926 when you attended, didn't you?

No, we just played, we was in Mexico about a little over a month between boats. You see, the boat schedule was slow at that time. And we stood a little over because we had so many engagements to play. One night they had just taken us a picture and they had to have a cabaret scene in it. By us having a band there, they gave us a little part in that. I think we made 20 hours just to play one song in that scene, the cabaret scene, in a nightclub there.
Was that a moving picture?
Yeah, yeah.
You don't know the name of that picture.
No, I know. No, they're fine. I know.
Well, where did you go to next?
Well, I came back to New Orleans.
Came back to New Orleans. Where did you play then?

Well, after that I went to New York in 1926. You were in New York. I played around New Orleans, went to New York. That's where I joined my sister, Lizzie Miles, international Creole song boy. She's known all over the world. So as I said before, it was Cliff Jackson's band. We used to broadcast over at WMCA nightly. We had a swell flow show there. I worked there for quite a while. After that job closed, I got homesick for the old New Orleans. So I could come back and play some more good jazz. I was just blowing and couldn't get used to those fellows the way they play. And they wanted you to play the way they want. And you can't play music that way. It's best to play the way you feel and the way you cut out to play. Whatever type of music you prefer, that's what you should stick at. Don't try to play like somebody else.
Well, did you ever play at any other time with your sister besides that New York engagement?

No, that was the only time because she had left here since I was a kid and she's traveled all over the world. She's internationally known. You worked with her approximately how long? Well, in New York? About eight months. About eight months. Yeah, about eight months.
Well, you came back to New Orleans in 1927. Yeah, came back. And you played here until about 1929.
Yeah, that's when I went.
And then you hit Chicago.
Went to Chicago, first time.
What was your first engagement there, Herb? In Chicago?

Yeah. Well, that's hard to tell, my first engagement, because I had to make myself known. I wasn't known at all in Chicago. I see. See, so I say my first engagement were recording with Baby Dots and Johnny Dots and Frank Melrose, piano player.
You have to remember the name of that recording.
Yeah, that's Fortin' Tight and Piggy Wiggly. I see. That was my first recording, as I mentioned before. Yeah.
And what was your next job there, or who else did you play with?

Well, after I got to be known, me and Bobby Jones, we formed a band, and we got quite a few jobs playing for different clubs. And Bobby Jones, we had about eight pieces. We also had a studio in Chicago.
Was Bobby Jones a New Orleans man, too?
No, he's a Chicago boy. He played sax, tenor sax.
Herb, what was your next record recording date after the first Dard session?

Well, I made another record with Paramount. I made St. James and the Farmery and the Wailing Blues. We had a combination of white accordion player, Joe Wiggins on alto sax, myself on trumpet, Thomas Till on drums, and Frank Melrose on piano. And Tom also blew the Frisco whistle. And that record, I loaned it to a friend of mine, and I never did locate that record again. I'm sorry to lose that out of my collection. Of course, maybe I could locate one somewhere. But at that time, they were selling for 35 cents, and they have become a collector's item now.
Herb, were you ever present at any of those famous Chicago recording sessions like the Hot Fives or any of the Oliver sessions? No.

The only one I was present at was Bob Crossby. They had a recording session before us. We came on after them, and them fellas was really small guys. They had a case of scotch and soda, and they had heard a whole lot of talk of the Harlem Ham Fats, so they invited us in the studio, and we drank, listened at them recording. And after they finished, we started recording, and they stood a while and heard us a while. Now, getting back to the Navy Pinnah, Bob Crossby and his full crew chartered the boat that I used to play on, Steamship North Show. I said make trips for half an hour on the lake, so they chartered the boat that night. So after they came on, well, it was off that night, so Bob Crossby came to me and asked me what I care to sit in, and at that time they called it Jam with the Boys, since we were from New Orleans. So me and Oliver Alcorn, tennis sax man, he picked us two out. He didn't take the rest of the boys. So we really had a real New Orleans session. I can't describe it. They took pictures, moving pictures, and I've never had a chance to see one of them. Somebody's got them somewhere. I'd sure like to see one of them. And we really had a session. Bob Zerke, the piano, he's dead now. Miller, for Zola, he's dead too. And had a young trumpet player, I think that made all the famous recordings. He had two trumpets. And we started slinging some real New Orleans stuff. And I really enjoyed Bob Crossby asking me to sit in with such a great band. And I don't think you'll go nowhere in New Orleans or anywhere and find a better jazz band than Bob Crossby, the original.
Well, tell me, did you play with Crossby at any other time, any later date? No, no.
That was the only time with Crossby.
I understand there was a dinner given in your honor and other jazz musicians in Chicago in 1935. Is that so?

Yeah, that was when I was at Tornis. I worked there a year and a half with little Joe Lindsey and his band. And Tornis was the headquarters for all greats like Lewis, Cab Calloway, Duke Ellington. And I have pictures of all that. Well, whenever they'd be in town, Tornis would invite them down. And Joe Lindsey used to be Lewis Armstrong's right-hand man, as they call it. And Lewis, all those greats would come there. And I used to play for them. And they'd sit down and enjoy. I have pictures on all that. And the last big party we had happened to be Lewis Armstrong, Duke Ellington, and Cab Calloway was in Chicago all at one time. And that's very odd. When Lewis was in New York, Cab might be in California or Duke might be in some other place. But that night, the whole three of them was in town, and Tornis gave a big blowout for them. And we really had a swell time.
All right. At that time, too, columnists began to refer to you as Louis Armstrong's stepson, more or less. Yeah, yeah.
I used to call him that.
I used to.

Well, maybe some passages I might sound like Lurie's, but I wasn't impersonating them just the way I felt. We all have that same New Orleans jazz spirit in us. But I've never copped after no other trumpet player.
What sort of relations were there between you and Louis? Did you, was he a personal friend of yours in the old days? Or?

Oh, no. I didn't know Lewis until Chicago, until I met him in Chicago. He used to live right in the next block from me on South Park near 35th Street. And whenever he'd come in, he'd say, Louis is always glad to meet New Orleans musicians or anybody from New Orleans, any kind of people. So I used to go visit him, and by me playing with Little Joe Lindsey, his right-hand man, him and Little Joe Lindsey was raised up together. And Lurie used to treat me swell, and so I got to know him, and he autographed many pictures that I have in my collection. I have some great pictures of him that he gave me.
Well, in 1936, Herb, as you said before, you recorded for Deck of Records. That was in Chicago.

Yeah, in Chicago. And then we had a session in New York in 1938. That's where we made the Viper song. If you were Viper, we left Chicago and went to New York. We made those records in New York at a three session. We stood there for about three days.
I see, and that was the only time you were in New York up until about 1941 or 42, wasn't it?
Yeah, you know, before I played at Capital Palace.
Yeah. And what were some of your other dates, or where else did you play between 1936 and 1940, or about 41?

I came back to Chicago, you see, after I left New York. I was stationed there in Chicago, but we just went to New York for that recording session. On top of the Decker studio had moved, discontinued in Chicago for the time being. So we had to go to New York to make the Decker records.
I see. Well, Herb, what else were you doing about 1937 or 38? Can you tell us something of your experience?

Well, I was in Chicago, playing with different bunches, you know what I mean? I played on Clark Street at the Firehouse. Many jazz fans used to come there and have me to play the blues all night. They'd come in, I mean white jazz fans, they'd come in and treat me well, just to hear the blues. Of course, around Chicago they didn't care much about the New Orleans blues. But they used to come in there and they really used to enjoy the blues. That's all they'd ask me to play. They liked blues in Chicago. The old Bauhaus, New Orleans blues. That's what they wanted.
In other words, the white people in the locality of Chicago and elsewhere were becoming aware of this music called jazz. Yeah. And they had certain forms that were interesting to them.
Yeah. And they could play it too because they'd come and sit in with us and play, you know what I mean? Quite a few of them.
Who were some of these people who sat in with you, Herb, and with whom you played? Did you ever come to them?

Well, you know, it slips your memory. You know, you soon forget about names and you meet so many musicians. But, you know, just like if you'd be out and you'd know where there's a band playing, you'd go anywhere, you'd be introduced, you'd sit out. And then maybe you wouldn't see them for quite a while after, or the slip of, you know, the remembrance of them.

That was the era of time around when Benny Goodman and Mesereau and Dave Tuff and those musicians were in Chicago. Yeah, at that time, yeah. Did you know Mesereau personally? No, I didn't know him personally, no. As you mentioned, record collectors were becoming in existence at that time.
Oh, yeah. Plenty of them, yeah.
When did you leave Chicago, Herb? You mean to come back to New York?

Yeah. Well, I left when this country declared war. So I hadn't been home in 13 years at that time. My mother and father was living, so I decided to come home. I thought maybe I would be drafted, but I missed the draft by a couple of years. So I had a nice job playing on the north side in the nightclub. So I turned the job over to P.C. William, my drummer. And the proprietor of the place liked me so much, I just, I couldn't tell him I was leaving. I just left. I didn't tell him anything. I hate to do that, but I'd have a time getting away from him. So I left in 41 and came home and start playing with George Lewis. I worked with George Lewis a long time. George Lewis's jazz band.
Around that time, didn't you get an offer from Sidney Boucher to join him in Boston? A few years after that, at least.

Yeah, when Sidney came down here to play the jazz concert at the auditorium with Lewis Armstrong, he had a chance to hear me. He had a chance to hear me. At that time, I was playing with Walter Nelson. He is standing right behind me at the Silver Store at St. Bernard and in that street, I think, or 8 Court. And we was playing there with Walter Nelson, one of the greatest blues guitar players in New Orleans. I am playing with him right now at this time right now. He's standing right over me. Just happened to come in. And we was playing at the Silver Store and Sidney came in. And that's where Sidney had a chance to hear me. So he sat down and he asked me to play different numbers for him. And we played it for him. So he went back to New York, I think. So he got an opportunity to use me in Boston. Sent a telegram and everything, which was a great offer. But at that time, my mother was sick and I hadn't been home for so long. And I don't think it's a job in the world. I don't care how much money it would pay. And would make me leave my mother. And I know she felt bad if I leave. And I know if I get up in Boston, New York, it would be a long time before I come back again. And the doctor gave up. So I said, well, I'm going to stay down here. I'll have to turn down all offers. But I was doing nice during the war. It's playing.

in Mississippi, Gulfport, Mississippi, Biloxi, a place like that. And I was really doing good. So, I was really sorry that I couldn't make the trip to go up there. But it's one of them things, I wouldn't leave Mama and she's sick to go for it. No, nobody. Yes, I'm sure that was
rather an unfortunate circumstance because I'm sure if you had returned to Boston,

the world would be more jazz conscious. Yeah, I would have a great opportunity to get back in New York like I wanted to. Rather conscious of the fact that you're still putting... Since jazz came back so strong, I'd have a better opportunity than before.
Well, to sort of summarize this, or to end this, Herb, what were some of your most unusual experiences that you had in your career as a musician playing jazz? Well, I'll tell you,

when I came back from New York, Chris Kelly, I had a whole lot of music and I used to send him music. So, when I came back, they decided, at that time, they were starting to use two trumpets in the jazz band. So, Chris Kelly decided to use me. Well, I was playing second and most of the time, Chris Kelly would be having this fun walking around and talking with the ladies. Well, I'd be playing then. I'd let him play and I'd walk around. So, we had a ballet who were advertising one day and we happened to meet Rene. I think it was at Denver and Murray Street. At that time, Rene was in his full swing. Nobody could touch him in the Orleans, but one man, Chris Kelly. And that ace in the hole was the blues and the type of people, while we was playing that, they were crazy about the blues. So, it happened, we backed the trucks up back to back and we started to play and what happened? A shower of rain came down. And the band that would leave first would be declared the loser. That mean you run away. So, Chris said, he don't care if it's storm, he's not leaving. But the drummer, he passed his drums off the truck because he didn't want his hands to get wet and get ruined. So, we played in the rain and battled Kid Rene and Kid Rene left. And we all were soaking wet and we played in the rain. I'll never forget that accident. Tell us something about Big Eye Lord. He's known as Big Eye Lord. You call his full name, people wouldn't hardly know him. He used to play when I was a young man. He used to play in the alley, in the alley cabaret. That's right back of the St. Bernard Market on North Claiborne and St. Bernard's Treaty. That little cabaret was really red hot, red hot in those days. I guess that was around 1920 or before. Big Eye traveled with Freddie Keppett's Creole band for a while. Yeah, for a while.

Yeah. And he was also responsible for influencing quite a few of your clarinets, Bechet and musicians such as him. Yeah. He was a great clarinet man. He just about certainly don't recognize clarinet as a clarinet. Yeah, he was in the Orleans. Yeah. But he just have typified the Orleans, New Orleans jazz. Yeah, yeah. He's going when they say Big Eye Lord is
playing tonight. You can expect a big crowd.

segments.title: Birth, first cornet and lessons with Professor Chaligny
segments.summary: Interview opens at Morand's New Orleans home in 1950. He was born in 1905, got interested in music at about ten from bands around town, bought a cornet, played along with records, then took 25-cent Sunday lessons to learn to read.

segments.title: His first band at 15-16: house parties, advertising, brother on drums
segments.summary: Trumpeters typically formed their own groups for house parties and advertising dances. Morand's band had his brother on drums and the bassist Chester Zardis.

segments.title: Bands of his youth and the best trumpeters: Buddy Petit, Chris Kelly, Kid Rena
segments.summary: He lists the bands he remembered and says he played second to Chris Kelly. Buddy Petit was his favourite, for low notes, and Kid Rena had the high notes.

segments.title: Dance halls and street battles of bands
segments.summary: He names the public halls where bands played. Bands advertised dances from trucks and when they met in the street they battled, the last band standing winning.

segments.title: Chris Kelly the Blues King, and Buddy Petit's gift of a song
segments.summary: Morand played advertising jobs with Kelly, whom no band could touch with his blues. Buddy Petit gave him the song later recorded by the Harlem Hamfats.

segments.title: Playing house parties and later the public halls
segments.summary: His own group played house parties, with furniture cleared out, for birthdays, weddings and christenings. Later he played the public halls with other bands.

segments.title: Sticking to New Orleans jazz style; older players and clarinetists
segments.summary: Morand says he stayed with New Orleans jazz through swing and bop. Most older horn players have died, and he names clarinetist Albert Burbank.

segments.title: Buddy Petit: great but unrecorded, and sending Morand as substitute
segments.summary: Buddy Petit was a great trumpeter who never recorded. Always late, he sent Morand to cover jobs across the lake until he arrived on a later train.

segments.title: Stage-company tours, Jack Carey and the young Oliver's ballyhoo wagon
segments.summary: Out-of-town tours came before he left for Chicago. He remembers trombonist Jack Carey, the Tiger Rag story, and King Oliver advertising dances from a furniture wagon before leaving town.

segments.title: Manuel Manetta, Jelly Roll Morton gone, and picnics at the fairground
segments.summary: Professor Manetta inspired and taught Morand and still teaches today, playing trumpet and trombone at once. Jelly Roll had left town. Summer picnics at the fairground featured brass and string bands.

segments.chapter: Brass bands, funerals and working conditions
segments.title: Plenty of work: parades, halls and picnics
segments.summary: Morand played marching bands and parades. There was enough work from halls, house parties, parades and picnics that jazz musicians needed no outside job.

segments.chapter: Brass bands, funerals and working conditions
segments.title: Brass band versus string band: Tuxedo, Olympia, Imperial
segments.summary: Bands such as the Tuxedo (Celestin) had a brass band and a string band. Players doubled, the tuba on string bass, and strings meant banjo and guitar.

segments.chapter: Brass bands, funerals and working conditions
segments.title: How a funeral worked: march, burial and the second line
segments.summary: He describes the society funeral procession from hall to church to cemetery, the long wait, and the second line afterward, with its dancing and fighting. Slow church hymns and marches going, jazz tunes coming back.

segments.chapter: Brass bands, funerals and working conditions
segments.title: Funeral marches, street parades and brass band instrumentation
segments.summary: Slow dirges were doubled up in tempo after the funeral. He describes club parades with umbrellas, the instruments in marching bands, and the doubling between brass and dance bands.

segments.chapter: Brass bands, funerals and working conditions
segments.title: Wages in the old days
segments.summary: Parade pay was about three dollars top, advertising two dollars, and halls paid four or five dollars a band. The leader got a couple dollars more.

segments.chapter: Brass bands, funerals and working conditions
segments.title: Hall conditions: balcony bandstands, no floor shows, few singers
segments.summary: Halls offered straight bands with no floor shows, seldom a piano, and the band on a balcony. Morand recalls being allowed to sit up with his heroes. Musicians rarely sat in and only the trumpeter sang, if anyone.

segments.title: Leaving for Chicago in 1929 and hearing the New Orleans men there
segments.summary: He went to Chicago alone in 1929 and auditioned for Decca. He heard Louis Armstrong at the Sunset and Oliver at the Plantation and was nervous when asked to sit in.

segments.title: Forming the Harlem Hamfats and their personnel
segments.summary: Morand formed the Hamfats with piano, E-flat clarinet, the McCoy brothers, drummers and a bassist. Only he and the bassist were from New Orleans, so playing New Orleans style was hard.

segments.title: Recording Old Red for Decca and losing the royalties
segments.summary: He composed many Hamfats tunes. The band auditioned at Decca with Old Red, recorded it despite his advice to get a contract, made up Lake Providence Blues in the studio, and received no royalties.

segments.title: Hamfats dates, first Chicago records and the song he did not write
segments.summary: The Hamfats formed around 1936-37, after his early Chicago sessions (Piggly Wiggly) and a stint with Frank Terrace in Michigan. He did not write one of the songs but supplied the music.

segments.title: Other Chicago bands and how Chicago players took to New Orleans style
segments.summary: The Hamfats never played an engagement together outside recording. Chicago musicians liked New Orleans style but played fast, arranged music.

segments.title: Thirteen years in Chicago; New York in 1926 with Cliff Jackson
segments.summary: He was never used by Jimmie Noone. He stayed 13 years in Chicago, but first went to New York in 1926 to play with Cliff Jackson at the Capitol Palace. New Yorkers did not understand New Orleans jazz.

segments.title: Chicago jazz mixed with local musicians; why New Orleans men moved north
segments.summary: Jazz in Chicago was played by New Orleans men mixed with readers who could not play without music. Musicians left as New Orleans work slowed and Storyville closed.

segments.title: Chicago bands, Fazola, and the Oliver band at the Plantation
segments.summary: He lists organized Chicago bands and notes Fazola with Bob Crosby. The Oliver band at the Plantation was a real New Orleans cabaret band, packed nightly, with Oliver stomping his foot to start tunes.

segments.title: Playing on the Navy Pier excursion boat and Clark Street
segments.summary: He led a four-piece band of New Orleans men on a Navy Pier excursion boat and played Clark Street, where white Chicago musicians were playing jazz. He does not recall Tom Brown.

segments.title: Leaving New Orleans with Nat Towles' Creole Harmony Kings; stranded in Tulsa
segments.summary: His first band away from home went to Tulsa, where the job collapsed. A man offered a job at Devonport, Oklahoma, where the band played at an open-air pavilion and broadcast on radio.

segments.title: Playing at the airfield and taking airplane rides
segments.summary: The band played at the airfield to draw customers for plane rides. Morand played trumpet in the air and the pilot did stunts with Towles, who said afterward he had never had such a thrill.

segments.title: Oklahoma theaters, band split-up, and the offer to go to Yucatan
segments.summary: After Devonport the band played theaters across Oklahoma until the group split up. Towles' father offered a Yucatan carnival job, and Morand sailed with him since others feared the Gulf.

segments.title: Playing the Yucatan carnival and appearing in a Mexican film
segments.summary: The six-piece band with Charleston dancers was a sensation, playing against a Spanish band and serenading all night. Each man made about $500 in gold. They also played a cabaret scene in a film.

segments.chapter: Chicago years: recordings, Armstrong, wartime exit
segments.title: Back home, New York with Lizzie Miles and Cliff Jackson, then Chicago
segments.summary: He joined his sister Lizzie Miles in New York in 1926 with Cliff Jackson's band, broadcasting on WMCA for about eight months. He returned to New Orleans, then went to Chicago in 1929, and advises players to be themselves.

segments.chapter: Chicago years: recordings, Armstrong, wartime exit
segments.title: First Chicago recordings and the band with Bobby Jones
segments.summary: His first engagements were record dates with the Dodds brothers and Frank Melrose, then he formed an eight-piece band with Bobby Jones. He later made a Paramount session with accordion and Joe Wiggins.

segments.chapter: Chicago years: recordings, Armstrong, wartime exit
segments.title: Sitting in with Bob Crosby's band
segments.summary: He saw no famous Chicago sessions except Bob Crosby's. Crosby's crew chartered his excursion boat, then he and Oliver Alcorn jammed with them, his only time with Crosby.

segments.chapter: Chicago years: recordings, Armstrong, wartime exit
segments.title: Tornis with Little Joe Lindsey and his friendship with Louis Armstrong
segments.summary: He spent a year and a half at Tornis with Little Joe Lindsey, where Armstrong, Ellington and Calloway came by. He was called Armstrong's stepson, but says he never copied him; he first met Louis in Chicago.

segments.chapter: Chicago years: recordings, Armstrong, wartime exit
segments.title: Decca sessions in Chicago and New York, 1936-38
segments.summary: After Decca recording in Chicago, the band went to New York in 1938 for a three-day session when the Chicago Decca studio was closed. Then he returned to Chicago.

segments.chapter: Chicago years: recordings, Armstrong, wartime exit
segments.title: Playing blues at the Firehouse on Clark Street for white jazz fans
segments.summary: On Clark Street he played the blues all night for white fans who came to hear New Orleans blues, some of whom sat in. He does not recall their names, and notes record collectors.

segments.title: Leaving Chicago in 1941 and joining George Lewis
segments.summary: After 13 years away he left Chicago when war was declared, quietly leaving his job to his drummer, and came home to play with George Lewis' band.

segments.title: Sidney Bechet's offer to join him in Boston, turned down for his sick mother
segments.summary: Bechet heard Morand playing with Walter Nelson at the Silver Store and sent a telegram offering a Boston job. Morand declined to stay with his sick mother, working the Gulf Coast during the war, and now regrets it.

segments.title: Unusual experiences: the rain battle with Kid Rena, and Big Eye Louis
segments.summary: He tells of playing second to Chris Kelly and a street battle with Kid Rena that Kelly won in the rain. Asked about Big Eye Louis, he recalls his alley cabaret and travelling with Keppard's band.
